hints: Find the acceleration using $v = u + at$ with initial speed $u = 0$, final speed $v = 3.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and time $t = 10\text{ s}$.
Apply Newton's second law horizontally: the forward force is the horizontal component of the pull, $10\cos 15^\circ$, opposed by friction $F$: $10\cos 15^\circ - F = ma$.
Substitute mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ and your calculated acceleration to calculate $F$ to 3 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Calculate the acceleration of the particle from rest:
$$v = u + at \implies 3.5 = 0 + 10a \implies a = \frac{3.5}{10} = 0.35\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Apply Newton's second law horizontally in the direction of motion:
$$10\cos 15^\circ - F = ma \implies 10\cos 15^\circ - F = 2(0.35) = 0.7\text{ N}$$

Solve for the frictional force $F$:
$$F = 10\cos 15^\circ - 0.7 = 10(0.965926) - 0.7 = 9.65926 - 0.7 = 8.95926 \approx 8.96\text{ N}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
The particle starts from rest ($u = 0$) and reaches a speed of $v = 3.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in $t = 10\text{ s}$. Use the linear motion equation:
$$v = u + at$$
$$3.5 = 0 + 10a \implies a = \frac{3.5}{10} = 0.35\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Next, resolve forces horizontally. The $10\text{ N}$ pulling force is directed at $15^\circ$ above the horizontal, providing a forward horizontal component $10\cos 15^\circ$. Friction $F$ opposes this motion:
$$F_{\text{net}} = 10\cos 15^\circ - F$$

By Newton's second law, $F_{\text{net}} = ma$:
$$10\cos 15^\circ - F = ma$$

Substitute $m = 2\text{ kg}$ and $a = 0.35\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$10\cos 15^\circ - F = 2 \times 0.35 = 0.7$$
$$F = 10\cos 15^\circ - 0.7$$

hints: Resolve forces vertically in equilibrium: $R + 10\sin 15^\circ = mg$ to determine normal reaction $R$.
Use the limiting friction formula $\mu = \frac{F}{R}$ with $F = 8.95926\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Resolve forces vertically in equilibrium to find the normal reaction $R$:
$$R + 10\sin 15^\circ = mg = 2(10) = 20\text{ N}$$
$$R = 20 - 10\sin 15^\circ = 20 - 10(0.258819) = 20 - 2.58819 = 17.4118\text{ N}$$

Calculate the coefficient of friction using $\mu = \frac{F}{R}$:
$$\mu = \frac{8.95926}{17.4118} \approx 0.515$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Since the particle moves horizontally on the plane, there is no vertical acceleration. Resolve forces vertically to balance the upward and downward forces:
$$R + 10\sin 15^\circ = mg$$

Substitute mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$ and $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$:
$$R + 10\sin 15^\circ = 2 \times 10 = 20$$
$$R = 20 - 10\sin 15^\circ$$

Because the particle is sliding, the frictional force equals $\mu R$:
$$F = \mu R \implies \mu = \frac{F}{R}$$
